source.title: TopK Language Models
source.authors: Ryosuke Takahashi; Tatsuro Inaba; Kentaro Inui; Benjamin Heinzerling

record.tranche_reason: The study compares neuron-entropy measures in dense and TopK-activated language models as an indirect test of whether architecture affects neuron specialization; it does not reproduce the Qwen3 pole audit.
record.gate_note: Only V4 is tested, indirectly: the paper measures token and semantic entropy in dense and TopK models, and demonstrates steering with a selected neuron. It does not estimate the share of neurons with one or multiple jobs, test explanations on held-out activations, evaluate attribution graphs, or assess the classic Inception example. The reported language-model and downstream-task benchmarks are capability results, not neuron-interpretability results.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It builds a TopK-sparse transformer to be interpretable and reports how its neurons compare with a dense baseline on token and semantic entropy, plus selected steering and tracing examples. Entropy is a proxy, not a share of neurons with one main job, so the study does not measure what V4 names. The sparsity is also induced on purpose by the architecture rather than arising in standard models. No result bears on V1–V3 or V5–V7. The entropy findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that TopK LMs keep competitive language-modelling and benchmark performance with only a moderate increase in model size. They present the architecture as an inherently interpretable alternative to post-hoc SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a modified transformer with TopK activation built into selected layers and measures neuron entropy and steering; it does not use the original Qwen3 pole-audit procedure or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported entropy pattern varies with architecture and layer: TopK models have lower entropy than dense baselines, the wider TopK variant has lower entropy, and the final two non-TopK layers show increased entropy. TopK sparsity is set to k=64 in the main entropy comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: The TopK-sparse 24-layer LMs have lower mean token entropy than dense baselines (6–7 vs about 9.3–9.5 early and 8–9 late). Semantic entropy is also lower (3.0–3.7 vs 4.3–4.4). Entropy rises again in the final two dense layers. Appendix B reports the same pattern in 8- and 16-layer models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Imposing TopK activation sparsity during pretraining lowers per-neuron token and semantic entropy relative to dense models of the same depth, with modest perplexity cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Single selected low-entropy neurons in a TopK LM steer generation toward a hand-labelled concept. One 'work' dimension becomes selective across nearly all layers after about 10^3 training steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TopK-sparse LMs, individual neurons can act as causal concept-steering units that are consistent across layers.

record.problems: The evidence is from small-scale models (the paper describes its largest main experiments as approximately 1B parameters); entropy is an indirect specialization measure, not a count of interpretable neurons; the concept-steering and cross-layer tracing examples are selected examples; and numerical uncertainty values are not provided in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-related results omitted. Language-model and downstream benchmark results, and hyperparameter-ablation results about task performance, were not included because they do not measure neuron interpretability or the claim's predicted behavior.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or shares of neurons with one or two jobs.
No share estimates across dense or mixture-of-experts models or at scale. The largest model is about 1B parameters.
No InceptionV1 analysis and no test of recursive generalization.

No share of interpretable neurons, no comparison of tools, no vision models, and no test of whether messiness in standard models comes from architecture or regularization. The study only builds a new sparse architecture.
No attribution graphs or comparison with replacement models.
Neuron labels come from top-activating tokens and are never tested on predicting where a neuron fires.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations. Automatic labelling is left to future work.

missing.what: Entropy comparisons for 8-layer and 16-layer dense vs TopK models. Same pattern as 24-layer; figures only, no numbers in text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V4' labels are dropped. The study engineers sparsity into a new architecture and measures entropy, not the share of interpretable neurons in models. It does not show that messiness in existing models comes from architecture or weak tools. Its single-neuron results are hand-selected examples.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or estimates of the shares with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood poles.
No estimates of the claimed shares across dense and mixture-of-experts models or at scales up to trillions of parameters.
No analysis of InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.

The study compares entropy-based specialization in dense and TopK architectures, but does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons, study InceptionV1-sized vision models, compare tools, or establish the proposed 5% to 99% range.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
No test of whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: It treats single neurons in its own architecture as interpretable units (labels, steering, tracing) without measuring an interpretable-neuron share.

tranche.reason: Method paper that builds a TopK-sparse LM and reports its own entropy comparisons and steering showcases. Entropy is a proxy, not a share of neurons with one main job, so it does not test any version.

source_check.notes: All 9 rows match the text. Appendix B (Figs 6-7) reports the same lower-entropy pattern for 8- and 16-layer models; no row records it, but no version is linked. Table 2 caption cites neuron 21:1957 (energy), which is missing from the table. T6 would also be defensible, since the study does not rely on dense neurons being clean.
